video_title: The Winning Democrat Who Wants to Break Up Political Parties | The Ezra Klein Show
gist: Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand (D), who won by ~11 points and ran ~24 points ahead of Kamala Harris's 2024 Iowa result on an anti-party-duopoly pitch, explains his theory that the two-party system is the root 'corruption' behind policy failure, and his plan to push a single open primary plus approval voting through a Republican legislature. He also outlines a cross-partisan, faith-inflected governing style and concrete Iowa policy targets (radon, nitrates/wetlands, public land).

insights.claim: Democrat Rob Sand won the Iowa governorship by about 11 points, running 24 points ahead of Kamala Harris's 2024 Iowa margin and almost 30 points ahead of the 2022 Democratic gubernatorial nominee; the last Democrat to win the office was Chet Culver in 2006.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host)
insights.so_what: Signals that anti-establishment Democrats can flip deep-red Midwest states, relevant for modeling 2028 state and federal political risk and farm-state policy.
insights.quote: He won it by about 11 points. He ran 24 points ahead of Kla Harris in 2024.

insights.claim: Sand says he raised a record roughly $58 million for the Iowa governor's race with an average donation of about $150, and that over 3,000 Iowa Republicans were donors to his campaign.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Record small-dollar plus cross-party donor base suggests the anti-party brand has real fundraising pull, a template other candidates may copy.
insights.quote: We literally had over 3,000 Iowa Republicans who were donors to the campaign.

insights.claim: Sand claims he received more votes for Iowa governor than any candidate since World War II except in 1964, and that 30-40% of attendees at his 200 town halls were not Democrats.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Breadth of crossover support gives Sand leverage over a Republican legislature on his agenda.
insights.quote: Typically 30 to 40% of the people at my town halls were not Democrats.

insights.claim: Sand reframes Winneshiek County's swing from Obama +23 in 2008 to Trump +9 in 2024 as consistency: voters there reward outsiders who shake up politics and defy their own party, and it is the parties that changed whom they nominated.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Swing-county voters are anti-establishment rather than ideological, so outsider positioning, not party label, drives Midwest outcomes.
insights.quote: What if it was always that that county wants people who are going to shake up politics and that county's actually been consistent and the parties have been inconsistent in who they've nominated.

insights.claim: Ezra Klein frames Sand as part of a revived anti-party populist tradition (1920s progressive reformers), distinct from Democratic anti-corporate/anti-billionaire populism and Republican anti-immigrant/anti-elite populism.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host)
insights.so_what: A third populist strand could reshape campaign messaging away from attacking corporations, modestly lowering anti-business policy risk where it wins.

insights.claim: Sand argues the two-choice political system is the underlying cause of corruption and governing failure because politicians only need to be the 'lesser of two evils' to be reelected, so they demonize opponents instead of solving problems.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: If this framing spreads, electoral-system reform becomes a live state policy agenda that could change incumbency dynamics.
insights.quote: politicians and candidates have come to understand that getting reelected can be easy even though solving problems is hard because they don't have to solve problems to get reelected.

insights.claim: Sand uses a broad definition of corruption that includes power-seeking and failure to govern, not just theft, citing a Menlo, Iowa town clerk who stole $60-80K alongside general dereliction by officeholders.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Expect a Sand administration to frame audits and good-government reforms broadly, with heightened scrutiny of public spending.

insights.claim: Citing Katherine Gehl and Michael Porter's 'The Politics Industry', Sand argues the two-party system is a duopoly that, like Burger King and McDonald's as sole options, competes by attacking each other rather than serving customers.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: A competition-economics frame for political reform that resonates with business audiences and may attract business-funded reform campaigns.
insights.quote: If you had to eat hamburgers and you could only get them at Burger King and Mc in McDonald's, they would be telling you the other one is feeding you rat meat.

insights.claim: Ezra Klein cites the book 'Stealth Democracy', whose survey data show the public reads partisan conflict as evidence of corruption and cooperation as a signal of clean government; Sand agrees voters sense something is wrong without knowing exactly what.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host)
insights.so_what: Explains why visibly bipartisan candidates outperform; useful lens for forecasting voter reaction to gridlock.
insights.quote: Cooperation is a signal of things working in a kind of clean, good government way and conflict is a signal of at least a certain form of public corruption.

insights.claim: Sand says money in politics is a real problem, calling Citizens United one of the worst Supreme Court decisions, and wants Iowa to follow Montana and Hawaii in redefining corporate powers at the state level to circumvent it, but sees parties as the bigger problem.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: State-level limits on corporate political spending powers are spreading; companies with state political-spending programs should watch for Iowa legislation.
insights.quote: Citizens United was one of the worst Supreme Court decisions in our lifetimes.

insights.claim: Klein argues Congress now passes giant omnibus bills (Inflation Reduction Act, bipartisan infrastructure bill, CHIPS and Science Act) because filibuster workarounds give so few legislative shots on goal; he says they should have been something like 400 separate bills.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host)
insights.so_what: Federal industrial policy will keep arriving in large, lumpy packages tied to trifectas, increasing policy-reversal risk for subsidy-dependent sectors.

insights.claim: Iowa's film-office tax credit program gave unlimited 50% refundable and transferable credits on production spending, enabling abuses such as buying a 747 for one shot and reselling it, and a $250 six-week rental for an ordinary shovel; Klein's takeaway is that the scandal was what was legal.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
entities: Iowa film office tax credit scandal
insights.so_what: A Sand administration is likely to be skeptical of loosely designed transferable tax-credit incentives; incentive-dependent industries in Iowa should expect scrutiny.
insights.quote: They literally wrote a statute that gives people an unlimited amount of refundable tax credits

insights.claim: Sand criticizes state film tax credits in general as a race to the bottom: a state attracts one month of filming until another state lowers the floor with bigger incentives.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Supports a view that state film/production incentives have weak durable returns and may be cut by reform-minded governors.
insights.quote: So, it's always kind of just a silly wild goose chase.

themes.theme: Open primaries and approval voting plan

insights.claim: Sand's core reform plan is a single open 'people's primary' with all candidates on one ballot, advancing the top three to five to a general election decided by approval voting (as first used in Fargo, North Dakota).
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: If Iowa adopts it, it would be a high-profile test of approval voting statewide and could spread, weakening party control over nominations.
insights.quote: So then send the top three to five to the general election.

insights.claim: About a third of Iowans are independents who must join a party to vote in primaries; Sand calls this un-American because taxpayers fund the elections.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Large unaffiliated bloc is the political base for primary reform in Iowa.
insights.quote: if you're an independent voter in Iowa, which about a third of Ians are

insights.claim: Sand prefers approval voting to ranked-choice voting because ranked choice is confusing and delays results, and prefers top-three-to-five over California's top-two jungle primary, which still leaves a lesser-of-two-evils general election; he notes Alaska uses a top-four system.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Signals a fork in the electoral-reform movement away from ranked-choice toward approval voting.
insights.quote: rank choice is confusing and it delays results as we're seeing right now.

insights.claim: Klein is skeptical that electoral-rule reforms yield big governance gains, noting no large jurisdiction clearly shows dramatic improvement and that nationalized media and declining local news shape politics; Sand responds that structure matters and voters and candidates take time to adapt, citing Sarah Palin learning under Alaska's new system that insulting rivals cost her support.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host) / Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Reform benefits, if any, show up over multiple cycles; do not expect immediate behavioral change after adoption.
insights.quote: oh, when I insult other people and I'm rude, it actually just makes people like me less.

insights.claim: Klein notes New York City's ranked-choice mayoral primary incentivized Brad Lander and Zohran Mamdani to become allies rather than enemies.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host)
insights.so_what: Evidence that multi-choice systems change candidate behavior toward coalitions.

insights.claim: Because Iowa has no ballot referendum process, Sand's reforms must pass through two Republican legislative chambers; he points to Alaska and Maine as places where such reforms have support beyond Democrats.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Passage odds hinge on Republican legislators; watch the 2027 Iowa session for electoral reform bills.
insights.quote: We don't have referenda.

insights.claim: Iowa already has reform precedents Sand wants to build on: it created the first independent redistricting commission (still considered the gold standard) and a merit judicial selection process using commissions of half lawyers and half non-lawyers that give the governor a short list.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Institutional precedent raises the plausibility that Iowa could be an early adopter of new election rules.

insights.claim: Sand's leverage strategy: 11 Republican state senators sit in districts he won, nine of them up for reelection in 2028, and he will hold 100 town halls a year in their districts publicizing bills they refuse to send him.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Creates electoral pressure that raises the odds his popular agenda items pass in 2027-2028.
insights.quote: There are, I think, 11 Republican state senators who were in districts that I won 10 days ago. Nine of them are up for re-election in 2028.

insights.claim: Sand is publicly urging the Republican legislature to pass his entire popular campaign agenda so they can fight on different ground in four years, and is inviting every legislator who votes for a bill to its signing ceremony.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Raises odds of bipartisan Iowa legislation on water quality, radon and public land.
insights.quote: make it yours, and then find some different ground to fight on four years from now.

insights.claim: Iowa Republicans previously gutted the state auditor's powers while Sand held the office and moved to weaken the governor's office before he took power, though they have said a lame-duck special session to further weaken the governor is not planned.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host) / Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Executive-power erosion is a key risk to the Sand agenda; watch for any special session.

insights.claim: Sand intends to include Republicans and independents in senior administration roles, as he did in the auditor's office with people who had donated to his opponent, to stress-test his ideas.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Suggests a more centrist, less ideologically predictable administration, lowering tail-risk policy swings.

insights.claim: Sand believes focusing on areas of broad agreement builds trust and produces durable policy that won't be unwound when power changes, and that on divisive issues such as Iowa's six-week abortion ban this creates room for middle-ground solutions; Klein counters that this can entrench wrong policies.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Expect little near-term movement on hot-button social issues from the Sand administration; durability of policy is a stated priority.
insights.quote: a solution that actually meets reality and it isn't just something that becomes another tug-of-war when the other party takes power.

insights.claim: Klein observes that as bipartisan votes became rarer, legislators stopped consulting across the aisle, so Democrats now pre-test bills against their left flank but not against Republicans, weakening legislation; he suggests Democrats should red-team their own bills.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host)
insights.so_what: Partisan bill design raises the odds of reversal after power shifts; discount durability of party-line legislation.
insights.quote: You should actually have red teaming if you're a Democrat.

insights.claim: Sand cites Mitch McConnell's stated goal of making Barack Obama a one-term president as proof that rhetoric about national unity fails without structural reform forcing politicians to compete.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Frames his reform push as a structural fix, not rhetoric; national Democrats may adopt it.

themes.theme: Iowa policy agenda: cancer, water, land

insights.claim: Iowa has the highest radon levels in the U.S. (about 6x the average); radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer. A new law requires radon mitigation in new construction, and Sand proposes zero-cost mandatory yes/no radon test and mitigation (~$2,000) disclosures at every home inspection and sale.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Could materially boost demand for radon testing and mitigation installers in Iowa's existing-home market.
insights.quote: We have the highest radon levels in the country. Uh 6x average.

insights.claim: Sand wants the largest wetlands restoration ever attempted to filter cancer-linked nitrates from Iowa water, expand public land (Iowa ranks 49th), and retain young people who leave for outdoor amenities.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Implies land acquisition/conservation spending and potential pressure on agricultural nitrate runoff, relevant to Iowa farmland use and ag inputs.
insights.quote: I want to do the single biggest wetlands restoration uh that anyone has ever seen.

insights.claim: Sand plans to keep doing 100 public town halls per year as governor and to tell constituents candidly when something can't be done, which he says voters find refreshing.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: High-touch retail politics is part of his pressure strategy on legislators.

insights.claim: Sand's town halls opened by having Republicans, independents and Democrats identify themselves and applaud each other, then sing America the Beautiful together, which he did in every Iowa county twice, followed by handing the microphone first to a Republican.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: A replicable cross-partisan campaign technique other candidates may copy.
insights.quote: And we did this in every single county in Iowa twice in this campaign.

insights.claim: Klein identifies a return of a religious, morally framed left in the Democratic Party (citing Sand, Talarico and Adam Hamilton), and Sand says a major strand of Christianity focused on the Sermon on the Mount and Matthew 25 has been unrepresented in politics, costing Democrats.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein (host) / Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Faith-inflected Democratic messaging may widen the party's reach in rural and religious electorates.
insights.quote: And there's a big piece of Christianity that hasn't been represented.

insights.claim: Sand recommends 'Tinkers' by Paul Harding, Doris Kearns Goodwin's 'Team of Rivals', and the four Gospels.
insights.speaker: Rob Sand
insights.so_what: Team of Rivals pick reinforces his cross-partisan cabinet approach.
